claim: Three amino acid loop extension homeodomain transcription factors (TALE HD TFs) act as life cycle regulators in green algae and land plants.
source: Three amino acid loop extension homeodomain transcription factors (TALE HD TFs) act as life cycle regulators in green algae and land plants.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work in the introduction.

claim: In mosses, TALE HD TF regulators are required for the deployment of the sporophyte developmental program.
source: In mosses these regulators are required for the deployment of the sporophyte developmental program.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Mutations in OUROBOROS in the brown alga Ectocarpus result in conversion of the sporophyte generation into a gametophyte.
source: We demonstrate that mutations in either of two TALE HD TF genes, OUROBOROS or SAMSARA, in the brown alga Ectocarpus result in conversion of the sporophyte generation into a gametophyte.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through genetic analysis and phenotypic characterization in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in SAMSARA in the brown alga Ectocarpus result in conversion of the sporophyte generation into a gametophyte.
source: We demonstrate that mutations in either of two TALE HD TF genes, OUROBOROS or SAMSARA, in the brown alga Ectocarpus result in conversion of the sporophyte generation into a gametophyte.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through genetic analysis and phenotypic characterization in the manuscript.

claim: The OUROBOROS and SAMSARA proteins heterodimerise in a similar manner to TALE HD TF life cycle regulators in the green lineage.
source: The OUROBOROS and SAMSARA proteins heterodimerise in a similar manner to TALE HD TF life cycle regulators in the green lineage.
evidence: This is demonstrated through pull-down assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: TALE-HD-TF-based life cycle regulation systems have an extremely ancient origin.
source: These observations demonstrate that TALE-HD-TF-based life cycle regulation systems have an extremely ancient origin, and that these systems have been independently recruited to regulate sporophyte developmental programs in at least two different complex multicellular eukaryotic supergroups, Archaeplastida and Chromalveolata.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of similar systems in distantly related lineages that diverged over a billion years ago.

claim: TALE-HD-TF-based life cycle regulation systems have been independently recruited to regulate sporophyte developmental programs in Archaeplastida and Chromalveolata.
source: These observations demonstrate that TALE-HD-TF-based life cycle regulation systems have an extremely ancient origin, and that these systems have been independently recruited to regulate sporophyte developmental programs in at least two different complex multicellular eukaryotic supergroups, Archaeplastida and Chromalveolata.
evidence: This is inferred from the convergent evolution of similar regulatory systems in two distantly related lineages.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, plus and minus gametes express two different HD TFs of the TALE family called Gsm1 and Gsp1.
source: In the unicellular green alga Chlamydomonas, plus and minus gametes express two different HD TFs of the three amino acid loop extension (TALE) family called Gsm1 and Gsp1 (Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claim: When two Chlamydomonas gametes fuse to form a zygote, Gsm1 and Gsp1 proteins heterodimerise and move to the nucleus, where they orchestrate the diploid phase of the life cycle.
source: When two gametes fuse to form a zygote, these two proteins heterodimerise and move to the nucleus, where they orchestrate the diploid phase of the life cycle.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claim: Gsm1 and Gsp1 belong to the knotted-like homeobox (KNOX) and BEL TALE HD TF classes, respectively.
source: Gsm1 and Gsp1 belong to the knotted-like homeobox (KNOX) and BEL TALE HD TF classes, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claim: In Physcomitrella patens, deletion of two KNOX genes, MKN1 and MKN6, blocks initiation of the sporophyte program leading to conversion of this generation of the life cycle into a diploid gametophyte.
source: In the multicellular moss Physcomitrella patens, deletion of two KNOX genes, MKN1 and MKN6, blocks initiation of the sporophyte program leading to conversion of this generation of the life cycle into a diploid gametophyte (Sakakibara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sakakibara et al., 2013.

claim: The moss BEL class gene BELL1 is required for induction of the sporophyte developmental program.
source: Similarly, the moss BEL class gene BELL1 is required for induction of the sporophyte developmental program and ectopic expression of BELL1 in gametophytic tissues induces the development of apogametic sporophytes during the gametophyte generation of the life cycle (Horst et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horst et al., 2016.

claim: Ectopic expression of BELL1 in gametophytic tissues induces the development of apogametic sporophytes during the gametophyte generation of the life cycle in moss.
source: Similarly, the moss BEL class gene BELL1 is required for induction of the sporophyte developmental program and ectopic expression of BELL1 in gametophytic tissues induces the development of apogametic sporophytes during the gametophyte generation of the life cycle (Horst et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horst et al., 2016.

claim: P. patens KNOX and BEL proteins have been shown to form heterodimers.
source: P. patens KNOX and BEL proteins have been shown to form heterodimers (Horst et al., 2016) and it is therefore possible that life cycle regulation also involves KNOX/BEL heterodimers in this species.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horst et al., 2016.

claim: Ectocarpus has a haploid-diploid life cycle that involves alternation between multicellular sporophyte and gametophyte generations.
source: This alga has a haploid-diploid life cycle that involves alternation between multicellular sporophyte and gametophyte generations (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A mutation at the OUROBOROS (ORO) locus causes the sporophyte generation to be converted into a fully functional (gamete-producing) gametophyte.
source: A mutation at the OUROBOROS (ORO) locus has been shown to cause the sporophyte generation to be converted into a fully functional (gamete-producing) gametophyte (Figure 1B) (Coelho et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coelho et al., 2011 and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The oro mutation induces a phenotype that is essentially identical to that observed with the P. patens mkn1 mkn6 double mutant.
source: This mutation therefore induces a phenotype that is essentially identical to that observed with the P. patens mkn1 mkn6 double mutant, but in an organism from a distinct eukaryotic supergroup (the stramenopiles), which diverged from the green lineage over a billion years ago (Eme et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparison of phenotypes and supported by citation to Eme et al., 2014 for the divergence time.

claim: Stramenopiles diverged from the green lineage over a billion years ago.
source: This mutation therefore induces a phenotype that is essentially identical to that observed with the P. patens mkn1 mkn6 double mutant, but in an organism from a distinct eukaryotic supergroup (the stramenopiles), which diverged from the green lineage over a billion years ago (Eme et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eme et al., 2014.

claim: The ORO gene was mapped to a 34.5 kbp (0.45 cM) interval on chromosome 14.
source: The ORO gene was mapped to a 34.5 kbp (0.45 cM) interval on chromosome 14 using a segregating family of 2000 siblings derived from an ORO x oro cross and a combination of amplified fragment length polymorphism (AFLP) (Vos et al., 1995) and microsatellite markers.
evidence: This is a primary finding from genetic mapping experiments.

claim: Resequencing of the 34.5 kbp interval in the oro mutant showed that it contained only one mutation: an 11 bp deletion in exon six of the gene with the LocusID Ec-14_005920.
source: Resequencing of the 34.5 kbp interval in the oro mutant showed that it contained only one mutation: an 11 bp deletion in exon six of the gene with the LocusID Ec-14_005920, which encodes a TALE homeodomain transcription factor. (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from sequencing analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The gene Ec-14_005920 encodes a TALE homeodomain transcription factor.
source: Resequencing of the 34.5 kbp interval in the oro mutant showed that it contained only one mutation: an 11 bp deletion in exon six of the gene with the LocusID Ec-14_005920, which encodes a TALE homeodomain transcription factor. (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and annotation of the gene.

claim: Three additional life cycle mutants (samsara-1, samsara-2 and samsara-3) were identified through a visual screen of about 14,000 UV-mutagenised germlings.
source: A visual screen of about 14,000 UV-mutagenised germlings identified three additional life cycle mutants (designated samsara-1, samsara-2 and samsara-3, abbreviated as sam-1, sam-2 and sam-3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from a mutagenesis screen.

claim: The sam mutants closely resembled the oro mutant in that gamete-derived parthenotes did not adopt the normal sporophyte pattern of development but rather resembled gametophytes.
source: The sam mutants closely resembled the oro mutant in that gamete-derived parthenotes did not adopt the normal sporophyte pattern of development but rather resembled gametophytes.
evidence: This is based on phenotypic observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Young, germinating sam mutant individuals exhibited the wavy pattern of filament growth typical of the gametophyte.
source: Young, germinating individuals exhibited the wavy pattern of filament growth typical of the gametophyte and, at maturity, never produced unilocular sporangia (the reproductive structures where meiosis occurs; Figure 1A), a structure that is uniquely observed during the sporophyte generation (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: At maturity, sam mutants never produced unilocular sporangia.
source: Young, germinating individuals exhibited the wavy pattern of filament growth typical of the gametophyte and, at maturity, never produced unilocular sporangia (the reproductive structures where meiosis occurs; Figure 1A), a structure that is uniquely observed during the sporophyte generation (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Unilocular sporangia are reproductive structures where meiosis occurs.
source: Young, germinating individuals exhibited the wavy pattern of filament growth typical of the gametophyte and, at maturity, never produced unilocular sporangia (the reproductive structures where meiosis occurs; Figure 1A), a structure that is uniquely observed during the sporophyte generation (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ectocarpus biology.

claim: Unilocular sporangia are uniquely observed during the sporophyte generation.
source: Young, germinating individuals exhibited the wavy pattern of filament growth typical of the gametophyte and, at maturity, never produced unilocular sporangia (the reproductive structures where meiosis occurs; Figure 1A), a structure that is uniquely observed during the sporophyte generation (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ectocarpus biology.

claim: The sam mutants exhibited a stronger negative phototrophic response to unilateral light than wild type sporophytes.
source: Moreover, the sam mutants exhibited a stronger negative phototrophic response to unilateral light than wild type sporophytes (Figure 2D), a feature typical of gametophytes (Peters et al., 2008) that was also observed for the oro mutant (Coelho et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A stronger negative phototrophic response to unilateral light is a feature typical of gametophytes.
source: Moreover, the sam mutants exhibited a stronger negative phototrophic response to unilateral light than wild type sporophytes (Figure 2D), a feature typical of gametophytes (Peters et al., 2008) that was also observed for the oro mutant (Coelho et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peters et al., 2008 and Coelho et al., 2011.

claim: Genetic crosses confirmed that the sam mutants were fully functional (i.e. gamete-producing) gametophytes.
source: Genetic crosses confirmed that the sam mutants were fully functional (i.e. gamete-producing) gametophytes and complementation analysis indicated that the mutations were not located at the same genetic locus as the oro mutation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on genetic crossing experiments.

claim: Complementation analysis indicated that the sam mutations were not located at the same genetic locus as the oro mutation.
source: Genetic crosses confirmed that the sam mutants were fully functional (i.e. gamete-producing) gametophytes and complementation analysis indicated that the mutations were not located at the same genetic locus as the oro mutation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on genetic complementation analysis.

claim: Hybrid sporophytes that were heterozygous for the sam mutations failed to produce functional unilocular sporangia.
source: Interestingly, hybrid sporophytes that were heterozygous for the sam mutations failed to produce functional unilocular sporangia.
evidence: This is based on phenotypic observations of genetic crosses.

claim: Wild type unilocular sporangia contain about a hundred haploid meio-spores produced by a single meiotic division followed by several rounds of mitotic divisions.
source: Wild type unilocular sporangia contain about a hundred haploid meio-spores produced by a single meiotic division followed by several rounds of mitotic divisions, whereas unilocular sporangia of SAM/sam heterozygotes never contained more than four nuclei indicating that abortion was either concomitant with or closely followed meiosis (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ectocarpus biology and confirmed by observations in Figure 2F.

claim: Unilocular sporangia of SAM/sam heterozygotes never contained more than four nuclei.
source: Wild type unilocular sporangia contain about a hundred haploid meio-spores produced by a single meiotic division followed by several rounds of mitotic divisions, whereas unilocular sporangia of SAM/sam heterozygotes never contained more than four nuclei indicating that abortion was either concomitant with or closely followed meiosis (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on microscopic observations shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No meiotic defects were observed in heterozygous sporophytes carrying the oro mutation.
source: Note that no meiotic defects were observed in heterozygous sporophytes carrying the oro mutation.
evidence: This is based on phenotypic observations.

claim: Ectocarpus sporophytes produce a diffusible factor that induces gametophyte initial cells or protoplasts of mature gametophyte cells to switch to the sporophyte developmental program.
source: Ectocarpus sporophytes produce a diffusible factor that induces gametophyte initial cells or protoplasts of mature gametophyte cells to switch to the sporophyte developmental program (Arun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arun et al., 2013.

claim: The oro mutant is not susceptible to the diffusible factor produced by sporophytes.
source: The oro mutant is not susceptible to this diffusible factor (oro protoplasts regenerate as gametophytes in sporophyte-conditioned medium) indicating that ORO is required for the diffusible factor to direct deployment of the sporophyte developmental pathway (Arun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arun et al., 2013.

claim: ORO is required for the diffusible factor to direct deployment of the sporophyte developmental pathway.
source: The oro mutant is not susceptible to this diffusible factor (oro protoplasts regenerate as gametophytes in sporophyte-conditioned medium) indicating that ORO is required for the diffusible factor to direct deployment of the sporophyte developmental pathway (Arun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the resistance of oro mutants to the diffusible factor and supported by citation to Arun et al., 2013.

claim: The sam-1 mutant is resistant to the action of the diffusible factor produced by sporophytes.
source: We show here that the sam-1 mutant is also resistant to the action of the diffusible factor.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Congo red staining of individuals regenerated from sam-1 protoplasts that had been treated with the diffusible factor detected no sporophytes.
source: Congo red staining of individuals regenerated from sam-1 protoplasts that had been treated with the diffusible factor detected no sporophytes, whereas control treatment of wild type gametophyte-derived protoplasts resulted in the conversion of 7.5% of individuals into sporophytes (Figure 2E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Control treatment of wild type gametophyte-derived protoplasts with the diffusible factor resulted in the conversion of 7.5% of individuals into sporophytes.
source: Congo red staining of individuals regenerated from sam-1 protoplasts that had been treated with the diffusible factor detected no sporophytes, whereas control treatment of wild type gametophyte-derived protoplasts resulted in the conversion of 7.5% of individuals into sporophytes (Figure 2E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Supplementary file 2.

claim: In order to respond to the diffusible factor, cells must possess functional alleles of both ORO and SAM.
source: Therefore, in order to respond to the diffusible factor, cells must possess functional alleles of both ORO and SAM.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both oro and sam mutants are resistant to the diffusible factor.

claim: The Ectocarpus genome contains two TALE HD TFs in addition to the ORO gene.
source: The Ectocarpus genome contains two TALE HD TFs in addition to the ORO gene.
evidence: This is based on genome sequence analysis.

claim: Resequencing of TALE HD TF genes in the three sam mutants identified three genetic mutations, all of which were predicted to severely affect the function of Ec-27_006660.
source: Resequencing of these genes in the three sam mutants identified three genetic mutations, all of which were predicted to severely affect the function of Ec-27_006660 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on sequencing analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The identification of three disruptive mutations in the same gene in the three independent sam mutants strongly indicates that these are the causative lesions.
source: The identification of three disruptive mutations in the same gene in the three independent sam mutants strongly indicates that these are the causative lesions.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic evidence.

claim: Ec-27_006660 was given the gene name SAMSARA (SAM).
source: Ec-27_006660 was therefore given the gene name SAMSARA (SAM).
evidence: This is a nomenclature assignment based on the genetic findings.

claim: ORO and SAM transcripts were most abundant in gametes.
source: ORO and SAM transcripts were most abundant in gametes (Figure 3A), consistent with a role in initiating sporophyte development following gamete fusion.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Transcripts of both ORO and SAM were detected in both male and female gametes.
source: Interestingly, transcripts of both ORO and SAM were detected in both male and female gametes indicating that gametes of both sexes carry both ORO and SAM proteins.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, GSP1 and GSM1 are expressed uniquely in the plus and minus gametes, respectively.
source: This situation therefore appears to differ from that observed in Chlamydomonas where GSP1 and GSM1 are expressed uniquely in the plus and minus gametes, respectively (Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claim: Genetic evidence supports a bi-sexual pattern of expression for ORO.
source: Whilst we cannot rule out the possibility that post-transcriptional regulatory processes result in ORO and SAM exhibiting sex-specific patterns of gamete expression, genetic evidence also supports a bi-sexual pattern of expression, at least for ORO, because complementation was observed when both male and female strains carrying the oro mutation were crossed with wild type strains (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on genetic crossing experiments.

claim: Sporophyte and gametophyte marker genes were down- and up-regulated, respectively, in sam mutant lines.
source: Quantitative PCR experiments demonstrated that sporophyte and gametophyte marker genes (Peters et al., 2008) were down- and up-regulated, respectively, in sam mutant lines (Figure 3B), as was previously demonstrated for the oro mutant (Coelho et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sporophyte and gametophyte marker genes were down- and up-regulated, respectively, in the oro mutant.
source: Quantitative PCR experiments demonstrated that sporophyte and gametophyte marker genes (Peters et al., 2008) were down- and up-regulated, respectively, in sam mutant lines (Figure 3B), as was previously demonstrated for the oro mutant (Coelho et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coelho et al., 2011.

claim: 1167 genes were differentially regulated between the sporophyte and gametophyte generations.
source: Comparative analysis of RNA-seq data for duplicate cultures of wild type sporophytes and wild type gametophytes grown under identical conditions (libraries GBP-5 and GBP-6 and libraries GBP-7 and GBP-8 in Supplementary file 9, respectively) identified 1167 genes that were differentially regulated between the two generations (465 upregulated in the sporophyte and 702 upregulated in the gametophyte; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 465 genes were upregulated in the sporophyte generation.
source: Comparative analysis of RNA-seq data for duplicate cultures of wild type sporophytes and wild type gametophytes grown under identical conditions (libraries GBP-5 and GBP-6 and libraries GBP-7 and GBP-8 in Supplementary file 9, respectively) identified 1167 genes that were differentially regulated between the two generations (465 upregulated in the sporophyte and 702 upregulated in the gametophyte; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 702 genes were upregulated in the gametophyte generation.
source: Comparative analysis of RNA-seq data for duplicate cultures of wild type sporophytes and wild type gametophytes grown under identical conditions (libraries GBP-5 and GBP-6 and libraries GBP-7 and GBP-8 in Supplementary file 9, respectively) identified 1167 genes that were differentially regulated between the two generations (465 upregulated in the sporophyte and 702 upregulated in the gametophyte; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The set of generation-biased genes was significantly enriched in genes belonging to 'Cell wall and extracellular' and 'Cellular regulation and signalling' categories.
source: The set of generation-biased genes was significantly enriched in genes belonging to two of the manually-assigned categories: 'Cell wall and extracellular' and 'Cellular regulation and signalling' and for genes of unknown function (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on functional category analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The set of generation-biased genes was significantly enriched for genes of unknown function.
source: The set of generation-biased genes was significantly enriched in genes belonging to two of the manually-assigned categories: 'Cell wall and extracellular' and 'Cellular regulation and signalling' and for genes of unknown function (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on functional category analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Enriched GO terms included several signalling- and cell wall-associated terms and terms associated with membrane transport.
source: Enriched GO terms also included several signalling- and cell wall-associated terms and terms associated with membrane transport (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The gametophyte-biased gene set was enriched for several cell signalling KEGG pathways.
source: The gametophyte-biased gene set was enriched for several cell signalling KEGG pathways whereas the sporophyte-biased gene set was enriched for metabolic pathways (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The sporophyte-biased gene set was enriched for metabolic pathways.
source: The gametophyte-biased gene set was enriched for several cell signalling KEGG pathways whereas the sporophyte-biased gene set was enriched for metabolic pathways (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The generation-biased genes included 23 predicted transcription factors.
source: We also noted that the generation-biased genes included 23 predicted transcription factors and ten members of the EsV-1–7 domain family (Macaisne et al., 2017) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the differentially expressed gene set.

claim: The generation-biased genes included ten members of the EsV-1–7 domain family.
source: We also noted that the generation-biased genes included 23 predicted transcription factors and ten members of the EsV-1–7 domain family (Macaisne et al., 2017) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the differentially expressed gene set and supported by citation to Macaisne et al., 2017.

claim: EsV-1–7 domain family members were significantly enriched in the sporophyte-biased gene set.
source: We also noted that the generation-biased genes included 23 predicted transcription factors and ten members of the EsV-1–7 domain family (Macaisne et al., 2017) (Supplementary file 3). The latter were significantly enriched in the sporophyte-biased gene set (χ2 test p=0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the differentially expressed gene set.

claim: Both the sporophyte-biased and the gametophyte-biased datasets were enriched in genes that were predicted to encode secreted proteins.
source: Both the sporophyte-biased and the gametophyte-biased datasets were enriched in genes that were predicted to encode secreted proteins (Fisher's Exact Test p=2.02e−8 and p=4.14e−6, respectively; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of predicted protein localization.

claim: Mutation of either ORO or SAM leads to upregulation of gametophyte generation genes and down-regulation of sporophyte generation genes.
source: Figure 3F shows that mutation of either ORO or SAM leads to upregulation of gametophyte generation genes and down-regulation of sporophyte generation genes, consistent with the switch from sporophyte to gametophyte phenotypic function.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: oro and sam mutants exhibited similar patterns of gene expression.
source: Moreover, oro and sam mutants exhibited similar patterns of expression but the patterns were markedly different to that of the imm mutant.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The gene expression patterns of oro and sam mutants were markedly different to that of the imm mutant.
source: Moreover, oro and sam mutants exhibited similar patterns of expression but the patterns were markedly different to that of the imm mutant.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ORO and SAM are master regulators of the gametophyte-to-sporophyte transition.
source: Taken together with the morphological and reproductive phenotypes of the oro and sam mutants, this analysis supports the conclusion that ORO and SAM are master regulators of the gametophyte-to-sporophyte transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined genetic, phenotypic, and gene expression data.

claim: The ORO and SAM proteins are capable of forming a stable heterodimer.
source: The ORO and SAM proteins were also shown to be capable of forming a stable heterodimer using an in vitro pull-down approach (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The interaction between the ORO and SAM proteins was mediated by their homeodomains.
source: Deletion analysis indicated that the interaction between the two proteins was mediated by their homeodomains.
evidence: This is based on deletion analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: All brown algae possess three HD TFs, all of the TALE class, including orthologues of ORO and SAM.
source: Analysis of sequence databases indicated that all brown algae possess three HD TFs, all of the TALE class, including orthologues of ORO and SAM (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on sequence database analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Comparison of brown algal ORO and SAM orthologues identified conserved domains both upstream and downstream of the HDs in both ORO and SAM.
source: Comparison of brown algal ORO and SAM orthologues identified conserved domains both upstream and downstream of the HDs in both ORO and SAM (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The conserved domains in ORO and SAM do not correspond to any known domains in public domain databases.
source: These domains do not correspond to any known domains in public domain databases and were not found in any other proteins in the public sequence databases.
evidence: This is based on database searches.

claim: The HD was the only domain that was common to both the ORO and SAM proteins.
source: The HD was the only domain that was common to both the ORO and SAM proteins (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on domain analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Only one non-brown-algal protein, from the raphidophyte Heterosigma akashiwo, possessed similarity to ORO and SAM protein domains.
source: Only one non-brown-algal protein, from the raphidophyte Heterosigma akashiwo, possessed similarity to these domains, allowing it to be classed tentatively as an ORO orthologue (gene identifier 231575mod; Figure 5A,C, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity searches shown in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: The origin of ORO can be traced back to the common ancestor with the raphidophytes (about 360 Mya).
source: This analysis allowed the origin of ORO to be traced back to the common ancestor with the raphidophytes (about 360 Mya; Brown and Sorhannus, 2010) but the rate of divergence of the non-HD regions of ORO and SAM precluded the detection of more distantly related orthologues.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of ORO orthologues and supported by citation to Brown and Sorhannus, 2010 for the divergence time.

claim: The rate of divergence of the non-HD regions of ORO and SAM precluded the detection of more distantly related orthologues.
source: This analysis allowed the origin of ORO to be traced back to the common ancestor with the raphidophytes (about 360 Mya; Brown and Sorhannus, 2010) but the rate of divergence of the non-HD regions of ORO and SAM precluded the detection of more distantly related orthologues.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Two TALE HD TFs, which are capable of forming a heterodimer, are required for the deployment of the sporophyte program during the life cycle of the brown alga Ectocarpus.
source: The analysis presented here demonstrates that two TALE HD TFs, which are capable of forming a heterodimer, are required for the deployment of the sporophyte program during the life cycle of the brown alga Ectocarpus.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: More than a billion years of evolution separate the brown algae and land plant lineages.
source: The parallels with life cycle regulation in the green lineage, where TALE HD TFs have also been shown to regulate deployment of the sporophyte program (Horst et al., 2016; Sakakibara et al., 2013), are striking. Knockout of the KNOX class TALE HD TF genes MKN1 and MKN6 in Physcomitrella patens result in conversion of the sporophyte generation into a functional gametophyte (Sakakibara et al., 2013), essentially the same phenotype as that observed with Ectocarpus oro or sam mutants despite the fact that more than a billion years of evolution separate the two lineages (Eme et al., 2014) and that the two lineages independently evolved complex multicellularity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eme et al., 2014.

claim: The brown algae and land plant lineages independently evolved complex multicellularity.
source: The parallels with life cycle regulation in the green lineage, where TALE HD TFs have also been shown to regulate deployment of the sporophyte program (Horst et al., 2016; Sakakibara et al., 2013), are striking. Knockout of the KNOX class TALE HD TF genes MKN1 and MKN6 in Physcomitrella patens result in conversion of the sporophyte generation into a functional gametophyte (Sakakibara et al., 2013), essentially the same phenotype as that observed with Ectocarpus oro or sam mutants despite the fact that more than a billion years of evolution separate the two lineages (Eme et al., 2014) and that the two lineages independently evolved complex multicellularity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolution of multicellularity.

claim: The similarities between life cycle regulators in the brown algae and green lineages suggests that they are derived from a common ancestral system that would date back to early eukaryotic evolution.
source: The similarities between life cycle regulators in the two eukaryotic supergroups suggests that they are derived from a common ancestral system that would therefore date back to early eukaryotic evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the convergent evolution of similar systems in distantly related lineages.

claim: Distantly-related homeodomain or homeodomain-like proteins act as mating type factors in both fungi and social amoebae.
source: The ancient origin of this life cycle regulatory system is further supported by the fact that distantly-related homeodomain or homeodomain-like proteins act as mating type factors in both fungi and social amoebae (Hedgethorne et al., 2017; Hull et al., 2005; Nasmyth and Shore, 1987; Van Heeckeren et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hedgethorne et al., 2017; Hull et al., 2005; Nasmyth and Shore, 1987; Van Heeckeren et al., 1998.

claim: In Basidiomycetes, homeodomain proteins regulate multiple aspects of sexual development including the formation of filaments, basidia and spores.
source: Moreover, in Basidiomycetes these proteins regulate multiple aspects of sexual development including the formation of filaments, basidia and spores indicating recurrent recruitment as developmental regulators (Banham, 1995; Hull et al., 2005; Kämper et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banham, 1995; Hull et al., 2005; Kämper et al., 1995.

claim: The ancestral function of homeodomain-based life cycle regulators was to detect syngamy and to implement processes specific to the diploid phase of the life cycle such as repressing gamete formation and initiating meiosis.
source: It has been proposed that the ancestral function of homeodomain-based life cycle regulators was to detect syngamy and to implement processes specific to the diploid phase of the life cycle such as repressing gamete formation and initiating meiosis (Perrin, 2012 and references therein).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perrin, 2012.

claim: Modifications to homeodomain-based regulatory circuits may have played an important role in the emergence of sporophyte complexity in the green lineage.
source: Indeed, it has been suggested that modifications to homeodomain-based regulatory circuits may have played an important role in the emergence of sporophyte complexity in the green lineage (Bowman et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bowman et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2008.

claim: The emergence and subfunctionalisation of two KNOX subfamilies early in streptophyte evolution is thought to have facilitated the evolution of more complex sporophyte transcriptional networks.
source: In particular, the emergence and subfunctionalisation of two KNOX subfamilies early in streptophyte evolution is thought to have facilitated the evolution of more complex sporophyte transcriptional networks (Furumizu et al., 2015; Sakakibara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Furumizu et al., 2015; Sakakibara et al., 2013.

claim: In the brown algae, the emergence of a multicellular sporophyte has not been associated with a marked expansion of the TALE HD TF family.
source: In the brown algae, ORO and SAM also function as major developmental regulators but, in this lineage, the emergence of a multicellular sporophyte has not been associated with a marked expansion of the TALE HD TF family.
evidence: This is based on the observation that brown algae possess only three TALE HD TFs.

claim: There has been considerable divergence of the ORO and SAM protein sequences during brown algal evolution.
source: However, there does appear to have been considerable divergence of the ORO and SAM protein sequences during brown algal evolution, perhaps reflecting the evolution of new functions associated with multicellular development and divergence of the sporophyte and gametophyte developmental programs.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and is speculative about the functional implications.

claim: Heterodimerisation appears to be a conserved feature of brown algal and green lineage TALE HD TFs despite the lack of domain conservation.
source: Heterodimerisation appears to be a conserved feature of brown algal and green lineage TALE HD TFs (Figure 4 and Lee et al., 2008) despite the lack of domain conservation.
evidence: This is based on experimental data in Figure 4 and citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claim: In Ectocarpus, heterodimerisation involves the ORO and SAM HDs.
source: However, in Ectocarpus heterodimerisation involves the ORO and SAM HDs whereas in Chlamydomonas, it is the KNOX1 and KNOX2 domains of Gsm1 that interact with the C-terminal region of Gsp1 (which includes the HD, Ala and DE domains).
evidence: This is based on deletion analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, it is the KNOX1 and KNOX2 domains of Gsm1 that interact with the C-terminal region of Gsp1.
source: However, in Ectocarpus heterodimerisation involves the ORO and SAM HDs whereas in Chlamydomonas, it is the KNOX1 and KNOX2 domains of Gsm1 that interact with the C-terminal region of Gsp1 (which includes the HD, Ala and DE domains).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work on Chlamydomonas.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, the Gsp1 and Gsm1 proteins are carried specifically by plus and minus gametes, respectively.
source: In Chlamydomonas, the Gsp1 and Gsm1 proteins are carried specifically by plus and minus gametes, respectively, so that dimerisation of the two proteins allows the organism to detect syngamy and therefore the transition from a haploid to a diploid state.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work on Chlamydomonas.

claim: In P. patens, both the class 2 KNOX proteins MKN1 and MKN6 and the BEL proteins BELL1 and BELL2 are expressed in the egg.
source: This also appears to be the case in P. patens, where both the class 2 KNOX proteins MKN1 and MKN6 and the BEL proteins BELL1 and BELL2 are expressed in the egg (Horst et al., 2016; Sakakibara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Horst et al., 2016; Sakakibara et al., 2013.

claim: Novel mechanisms may lead to the activation of TALE HD TF life cycle regulators in groups that have evolved complex multicellularity.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that novel mechanisms may lead to the activation of TALE HD TF life cycle regulators in groups that have evolved complex multicellularity.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences in expression patterns between unicellular and multicellular organisms.

claim: In P. patens, the glutamate receptor GLR2 may be a component of a mechanism that activates TALE HD TF life cycle regulators.
source: In P. patens, the glutamate receptor GLR2 may be a component of such a mechanism (Ortiz-Ramírez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ortiz-Ramírez et al., 2017.

claim: Modified regulation of TALE HD TFs may have had advantages in terms of life cycle flexibility.
source: Moreover, modified regulation of these TALE HD TFs may have had advantages in terms of life cycle flexibility.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about evolutionary advantages.

claim: In Ectocarpus, it would not be possible to deploy the sporophyte program in parthenogenetic gametes if gamete fusion was strictly required to create an ORO-SAM heterodimer.
source: For example, in Ectocarpus, it would not be possible to deploy the sporophyte program in parthenogenetic gametes if gamete fusion was strictly required to create an ORO-SAM heterodimer.
evidence: This is logical inference about the implications of the regulatory mechanism.

claim: Diploid sporophytes heterozygous for sam mutations exhibited abortive development of unilocular sporangia at a stage corresponding to the meiotic division of the mother cell.
source: Interestingly, diploid sporophytes heterozygous for sam mutations exhibited abortive development of unilocular sporangia at a stage corresponding to the meiotic division of the mother cell.
evidence: This is based on phenotypic observations shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The ORO SAM system may have originally evolved as a global regulator of diploid phase processes.
source: However, these phenotypes make more sense when viewed from an evolutionary perspective, if the ORO SAM system originally evolved as a global regulator of diploid phase processes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the evolutionary origins of the system.

claim: There is accumulating evidence for an ancient role for HD TFs in life cycle regulation in both the bikont and unikont branches of the eukaryotic tree of life.
source: There is now accumulating evidence for an ancient role for HD TFs in life cycle regulation in both the bikont and unikont branches of the eukaryotic tree of life (Hedgethorne et al., 2017; Horst et al., 2016; Hull et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2008; Sakakibara et al., 2013 and this study).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and the current study.

claim: HD TF-based life cycle regulatory systems have been adapted to coordinate life cycle progression and development in at least two multicellular eukaryotic lineages (land plants and brown algae).
source: We show here that these systems have been adapted to coordinate life cycle progression and development in at least two multicellular eukaryotic lineages (land plants and brown algae).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data.

claim: The recruitment of TALE HD TFs as sporophyte program master regulators in both the brown and green lineages represents an example of latent homology.
source: The recruitment of TALE HD TFs as sporophyte program master regulators in both the brown and green lineages represents a particularly interesting example of latent homology, where the shared ancestral genetic toolkit constrains the evolutionary process in two diverging lineages leading to convergent evolution of similar regulatory systems (Nagy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citation to Nagy et al., 2014.

claim: The shared ancestral genetic toolkit constrains the evolutionary process in two diverging lineages leading to convergent evolution of similar regulatory systems.
source: The recruitment of TALE HD TFs as sporophyte program master regulators in both the brown and green lineages represents a particularly interesting example of latent homology, where the shared ancestral genetic toolkit constrains the evolutionary process in two diverging lineages leading to convergent evolution of similar regulatory systems (Nagy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nagy et al., 2014.

claim: The oro mutation has been shown to behave as a single-locus, recessive, Mendelian factor.
source: The oro mutation has been shown to behave as a single-locus, recessive, Mendelian factor (Coelho et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coelho et al., 2011.

claim: Full-length transcripts of both the ORO and SAM genes are produced during the gametophyte generation.
source: This analysis indicated that full-length transcripts of both the ORO and SAM genes are produced during the gametophyte generation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq mapping analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the ORO and SAM proteins possess regions that are predicted to be highly disordered.
source: Interestingly, both the ORO and SAM proteins possess regions that are predicted to be highly disordered (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Intrinsically disordered regions are a common feature in transcription factors.
source: Intrinsically disordered region are a common feature in transcription factors and the flexibility conferred by these regions is thought to allow them to interact with a broad range of partners (Niklas et al., 2015), a factor that may be important for master developmental regulators such as the ORO and SAM proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Niklas et al., 2015.

claim: The flexibility conferred by intrinsically disordered regions is thought to allow transcription factors to interact with a broad range of partners.
source: Intrinsically disordered region are a common feature in transcription factors and the flexibility conferred by these regions is thought to allow them to interact with a broad range of partners (Niklas et al., 2015), a factor that may be important for master developmental regulators such as the ORO and SAM proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Niklas et al., 2015.
